AI Tools & Academic Integrity — Reference Guide for MM(DU) Faculty

A structured overview of how AI tools map onto academic work — research, teaching, writing, and the citation and ethics questions that come with using them — compiled as a standing reference for Maharishi Markandeshwar (Deemed to be University) faculty alongside the generators on this page.

Reference categoryWhat it covers
Institutionally Available AI ResourcesAI tools a faculty member may already have access to through university-held or department-held subscriptions, rather than a personal account.
Generative AI ToolsGeneral-purpose chat/generation tools (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot and similar) and how they differ.
AI Tools for ResearchLiterature discovery & synthesis: tools such as Scite, Elicit, Inciteful, Research Rabbit, Scholarcy, NotebookLM, and deep-research assistants for grant writing and literature review.
AI Tools for Teaching & LearningClassroom-facing tools for interactive presentations, lesson planning, grading assistance, and study aids for students.
AI Tools for Writing / Video / ImagesDedicated categories for writing assistants and generative media tools.
Using AI in ResearchUsing AI responsibly across the research lifecycle — literature review, data analysis, drafting. See the "Using AI in Research" tab above for the full breakdown.
Resources for EducatorsClassroom policy templates and guidance for instructors setting AI-use expectations.
How to Cite AI-Generated ContentCitation formats (APA/MLA/Chicago) for content produced with AI assistance.
Prompt DesignPractical prompting guidance for getting reliable output from AI tools.
AI and Ethics / Copyright / Publisher PoliciesEthical-use considerations, copyright status of AI output, and how individual academic publishers currently treat AI-assisted manuscripts.

How AI tools can be used in research

#UseWhat it does
1Generating Research IdeasAnalyses data to identify trends, gaps, and emerging topics, helping refine research questions and suggest angles by recognising patterns in existing literature or datasets.
2Finding Relevant InformationUses natural language processing to locate relevant articles, papers, and datasets quickly, and to surface high-quality sources by analysing content and citations.
3Data ScrapingAutomatically collects large amounts of relevant information from websites for analysis — an increasingly common way to assemble datasets from web sources.
4Generating Titles and SummariesHelps craft concise titles or generate summaries from long texts, assisting with abstracts or introductions.
5AI-Assisted Research WritingAssists in organising literature reviews, methodologies, and discussions with suggestions tailored to your writing style.
6Data AnalysisRecognises patterns in complex datasets, automates repetitive tasks like data cleaning, and generates predictive insights.
7Citation ManagementAutomatically organises references, generates bibliographies, and helps ensure adherence to style guidelines.

Limitations of using AI tools in research

LimitationWhy it matters
Bias and discriminationAI tools can inherit biases from their training data, leading to skewed outcomes — validate AI-generated content against credible sources to avoid perpetuating stereotypes.
Plagiarism concernsAI-generated content can resemble existing work, increasing plagiarism risk — originality and research integrity remain the researcher's responsibility.
Data misinformationAI tools may generate inaccurate data and information — always cross-check AI output against reliable sources before it enters your research.

AI for systematic review

AI tools are increasingly used throughout the systematic review and evidence-synthesis process. Their utility at each review stage is well documented, but so are their biases and weaknesses — copyright and intellectual-property considerations should stay front of mind. Selected peer-reviewed reading on the subject:

Which tool fits which university workflow

WorkflowBest-suited toolWhy
Teaching and Academics Claude / Claude Code, or Gemini (if already on Workspace) Strong structured long-form writing and easy iteration on a syllabus, unit plan, or course material; Gemini is the pragmatic default if the institution already pays for Workspace, since it's bundled at no extra cost. Purpose-built classroom tools (MagicSchool, Eduaide.ai — see the reference table above) are worth a look too if lesson-plan generation is the only need.
Evaluating / analysing student records Claude or Gemini for analysis and write-up; Perplexity if the task needs cited external comparison This is sensitive personal data — the deciding factor is data-handling terms and institutional agreements, not raw capability. Whichever tool is used should be covered by an institutional/enterprise agreement with clear data-retention terms, not a personal consumer account. Avoid routing student records through agentic tools (Manus, Devin, CrewAI) that browse the web or call external services mid-task.
HR-related work (policy drafting, correspondence, screening support) Claude or Gemini (Workspace) under an enterprise/team plan HR work is also sensitive-data territory — team/enterprise tiers exist specifically for the admin controls, audit logging, and data-handling commitments that HR use requires. Perplexity is a reasonable complement for researching current labour-law or policy context, with citations to verify.
Administration (scheduling, reporting, cross-department coordination) Gemini (if on Workspace) for day-to-day drafting; Claude for longer analytical documents; CrewAI only if the department has engineering support to build and maintain an automation Administrative work is usually about volume and integration with existing tools (email, sheets, calendars) more than raw model capability — this is where Workspace-bundled Gemini's native integration wins on convenience. Agent frameworks like CrewAI/AutoGPT/Devin can automate repetitive admin workflows but need real engineering time to set up and maintain safely; they're not a drop-in tool for non-technical staff.

Summary

CategoryTake-away
Cheapest genuinely capable optionDeepSeek's chat app is free with no paid tier at all; its API is also among the cheapest frontier-class pricing available. Best where budget is the binding constraint and data-residency policy allows it.
Best all-round academic fitClaude / Claude Code and Google Gemini — both have real institutional/enterprise tiers with the admin and data-handling controls university procurement typically requires, and both now bill genuine India pricing: Claude Pro at ₹2,000–2,399/mo, Gemini AI Pro at ₹1,950/mo.
Best for literature review / cited researchPerplexity (Deep Research) — citation-first by design; the official India Pro price is ₹17,000/year (≈₹1,417/mo), with a discounted Education tier available via SheerID verification for university users.
Autonomous coding / engineering delegationDevin and Cursor/Windsurf lead here, but both are usage-metered (ACUs or model quotas) — treat the advertised entry price as a floor, not the real monthly cost, and budget accordingly.
Multi-agent automationCrewAI and AutoGPT are free frameworks, not managed products — genuinely low-cost only where a department has the engineering capacity to build, host, and maintain the automation itself.
Watch for changeWindsurf was acquired by Cognition (Devin's parent) and rebranded "Devin Desktop" in June 2026 — a reminder that this whole landscape moves fast enough that any pricing table, including this one, needs re-verification before real budgeting.

Research · Draft Assistance

Research Paper Draft Generator

Generates a complete research paper draft, formatted like a published journal article, with real DOI-linked references pulled live from Crossref, black-and-white figures, and 12 copyable mathematical formulas with a genuine regression analysis — the section content still needs your own effort.

How this draft is built

Built using a real, open-source .docx engine — a genuine Word document, formatted to match a real published Springer Nature journal article (running header with page count, unnumbered section headers, hanging-indent reference list, a "DRAFT" banner). All figures render in black and white for print compatibility. Unlike the other generators on this page, the reference list is not template text: your topic is sent to Crossref — a free, public, keyless database of real published papers — to fetch genuinely existing, DOI-linked sources; peer-review records and entries with no listed author are filtered out automatically, so the list never falls back to showing "Anonymous" as if it were a real author. Sources are formatted as a real Vancouver-style reference list with in-text citation markers like [12] or [7, 19] pointing at them — real, relevant background papers, not a guarantee that each one supports every specific sentence next to its citation number, so read each one and cite it properly wherever it actually applies. The paper also includes 12 real mathematical formulas spread naturally through the Theory, Methodology, Results, and Discussion sections — each with its own lead-in, a full explanation naming every variable, and a stated purpose — rendered as real selectable, copyable, searchable text rather than images. A dedicated Regression Analysis subsection fits a genuine least-squares line to a sample of illustrative data and reports the actual computed slope, intercept, and R² — real statistics computed live from whatever is plotted, not fabricated numbers. If Crossref can't be reached, the reference list falls back to clearly labelled placeholder entries instead of ever inventing fake citations. The section prose, figures and tables remain illustrative template content either way, so review and rewrite them with your own research before submission.

Assessment · Draft Assistance

Quiz Generator

Generates a 30-question multiple-choice quiz — by default, straight from real Wikipedia content, no key needed at all.

Generation mode

Get one free at console.anthropic.com. Saved only in this browser (localStorage) — never written into the downloaded quiz file, never sent anywhere but the provider you picked above.

✓ key saved in this browser
How this quiz is built, and how to get a key from each provider

Default — no key needed: your topic is matched to a real Wikipedia article (a free, public, keyless lookup — the same approach the Mind Map Explorer above uses), and the questions are built as fill-in-the-blank items where the blank and the correct answer are lifted directly from real sentences in that article — a real fact, not an invented one, with three other real terms from the same article used as decoys. This means quality depends on how developed the Wikipedia article is: well-covered academic topics work best, and very obscure or narrow topics may return fewer than 30 questions, or fail to find an article at all. Review every question before handing it out — cloze-style blanks can occasionally be ambiguous or have more than one defensible answer out of context.

Optional — Use AI instead: switch the mode above to call an AI provider's API directly from your browser using your own key, so questions are freshly written for the topic rather than extracted from an article — useful for topics with thin Wikipedia coverage, or for a different question style. Each provider's key is stored only in this browser's local storage, in its own slot: never written into the downloaded quiz file, never sent anywhere else, and switching providers in the dropdown never touches the other two keys.

Google (Gemini) — try this first if you're out of credit elsewhere: go to aistudio.google.com/apikey and sign in with a Google account → click Create API key (choose or create a Google Cloud project if prompted) → copy the generated key (starts with AIza). Gemini has a genuine, ongoing free tier — no card, no expiry, generous daily limits — the only real "free" option of the three. It can still occasionally block direct browser requests (CORS) for some accounts; if so, try Anthropic instead.

Anthropic (Claude) — the most consistently reliable option here: go to console.anthropic.com and sign in or create a free account → open Settings → API Keys → click Create Key, name it anything, and copy the key (starts with sk-ant-). New accounts get a small one-time free trial credit (around $5, phone verification, no card needed) — once that's used up, add credit under Plans & Billing to keep going.

OpenAI (ChatGPT): go to platform.openai.com and sign in or create a free account → open API keys in the left sidebar → click Create new secret key, name it anything, and copy it (starts with sk-). OpenAI no longer gives free trial credit to new accounts, so a small top-up under Settings → Billing is needed before this key will work at all — and like Google, OpenAI also blocks direct browser requests for some accounts (CORS), so it may still fail even when funded.

Exam Question Paper Generator

How this question paper is built

Built entirely in your browser using the same real, open-source .docx engine as the research paper and notes generators above — no server, nothing uploaded. How this lab manual is built

Built entirely in your browser using the same real, open-source .docx engine as the other document generators on this page — no server, nothing uploaded. If a topic doesn't match anything in the library, that experiment gets a complete Aim/Theory/Algorithm section plus a clearly marked space for you to write and test your own code — this page will never invent source code or output that hasn't actually been run, the same principle used throughout this dossier. Each experiment starts on its own page, matching how printed and bound lab files are normally submitted. Review every matched experiment too: the code is verified and working, but check that it fits your exact syllabus wording and course conventions before printing.

Study Aid · Audio

Podcast Audio Generator (Hindi)

Type a topic — pulls a real Hindi Wikipedia article, shapes it into a spoken-style podcast script, and narrates it aloud using your browser's own built-in Hindi voice. No key, no login, no subscription, and no server involved.

Ready to play —

Show transcript text
How this works, and what it deliberately doesn't do

The script is built from a real Hindi Wikipedia article for whatever topic you type — the same public, keyless Wikipedia API already used by the Quiz Generator above, pointed at hi.wikipedia.org instead of the English edition — wrapped in a spoken-style Hindi introduction and conclusion. Narration uses your browser's own built-in speechSynthesis — a real, standard, W3C web platform feature, not a third-party service — with a Hindi voice if your system has one installed (most Windows/Edge installs do by default; if none is found, the page tells you rather than silently failing). "Record & Download Audio" is a best-effort feature: your browser will ask permission to share this tab's audio, which is the only standards-based way a webpage can capture synthesized speech into a downloadable file — if your browser doesn't support that, the transcript download still works every time. This deliberately does not use the "g4f" library (an unofficial tool that scrapes various AI providers without authorization) or "edge-tts" (which works by calling Microsoft's undocumented internal TTS endpoint) — both are fragile, unofficial workarounds rather than real, sanctioned APIs, and aren't something this page builds on.

15

Teaching · Course Scheduling

Lesson Plan Generator

Paste the syllabus and set a start and end date — generates a full teaching calendar mapping which topic gets covered on which date across the term, with a 2-week examination break built in, as a formatted MM(DU)-headed Word document.

How this is built

Every class day between the start and end date is identified first, using whichever weekdays you've ticked above. A 2-week examination break is then placed around the midpoint of that range and removed from the teaching days entirely — it appears in the schedule as a clearly marked non-teaching block, not skipped over silently. The remaining teaching days are then divided across your syllabus topics: if there are more class days than topics, a topic can span several consecutive class days; if there are more topics than class days, more than one topic is grouped onto the same day. Teaching method and expected outcome per topic are drawn from a varied set of standard pedagogical phrasings so consecutive topics don't all read identically. This is a structural starting point built from what you typed in, not a judgement on actual pacing — adjust dates and groupings to fit your own calendar, holidays, and university events before use.
